---
title: "14. Inspect and interact with a browser"
---

When an agent builds a research website or a report to read in a browser, it needs to inspect what readers will see and use. A page can contain valid code and still have an unreadable figure, a broken filter, or navigation that disappears on a narrow screen. Browser access lets the agent open the page, try its controls, and use what it finds to improve the work.

Suppose a results page plots population counts by region and lets readers choose a year. Selecting 2024 changes the selection shown, but the plot still displays 2023 results. The agent can investigate using the browser tools already available in its app. Another option is [`Playwright`](https://playwright.dev/), software that automates browser actions. After correcting the website code, the agent can reload the page and check that the plotted values and labels match the selected year.

## Set up browser access and choose the account {#choose-the-browser-account}

Ask the agent to check which browser tools it can use in the current session and configure another only if needed. [`Playwright MCP`](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright-mcp) is one option: it makes browser operations available through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard way for an agent application to discover and use tools. The project also documents a command-line option for agents that can run commands. [Chapter 13: Connect to research data and services: MCP](#service-connections) explains how to choose and configure a connection.

Have the agent install and configure any missing components using the chosen tool's documentation. A *browser profile* is a separate set of browser settings and saved login information. Where the integration supports it, have the agent use a separate profile for the task so it does not inherit your everyday signed-in accounts. If the task needs an account, identify which one and complete any personal sign-in yourself. The agent should explain the access it needs before using it.

A page's contents may be sent to a hosted large language model (LLM), which runs on the service provider's computers. Decide which material may be sent using [Chapter 3: Know where your data goes](https://dss-agentic-research.pages.dev/chapters/research-limits.html) in *Doing Research with AI Agents*. Have the agent configure the relevant controls from [Chapter 2: Control what added tools can access](#tool-access); a separate browser profile does not itself restrict every website or action. Submitting information or changing an online record should follow your authorization for the task.

## Inspect a research website

For a site under development, have the agent start a *local preview*: the website running on your computer for inspection in a browser. It should confirm that its browser can reach the preview. The site need not be published online for this check.

In the year-selection example, ask the agent to choose 2024, compare the displayed values and labels with the saved 2024 results, and then switch back to 2023. A screenshot can reveal clipped labels or overlapping elements; using the selector reveals whether it changes the plot. Have the agent fix any problems and repeat the affected checks after reloading the page.

::: {#prompt-check-website .prompt}
> Start this project's local website preview and open it using the available browser tools. On the results page, select 2024 and confirm that the plotted values and labels match the saved results for that year. Switch back to 2023 and check again. Try the main navigation and inspect the pages at desktop and narrow phone-sized browser widths. Fix problems and repeat the affected checks after reloading. Report the pages, actions, and widths checked, and show any remaining issue that needs my design decision. Save the preview and checking instructions in `README.md` and reuse them after relevant website changes.
:::

The agent should report what it actually checked, including any pages it could not inspect. A narrow browser window helps check layout but does not establish that the site works on every physical phone. These checks concern the website's presentation and behavior; you still assess the research choices and interpretation behind its results.

![](figures/browser-research.svg){#fig-browser-research fig-alt="In the first example, a website filter selects 2024 but the plot still shows 2023. The agent fixes the source, reloads and checks that the plot follows the filter. In the second, it inspects a public portal's release selector and download, then preserves the original data, source and release information, and collector script in a collection directory. These are distinct uses of browser access."}

## Collect data through a website

Browser access can also help the agent find data on an unfamiliar website. Suppose you need population counts for every region of a country in 2024 from a public statistics portal. The agent can inspect the release information, check the year and geographic coverage, and locate a download. If a suitable export or API is already known, it can use that directly.[^tk-browser-api]

Ask the agent to use a permitted collection method and confirm what the downloaded file contains. It should check the region identifiers, year, and population measure against the source documentation, compare representative values, and report missing or duplicate regions. A successful download alone does not establish that it contains the requested data.

Have the agent save the original download unchanged, together with its *provenance*: a record of where it came from and how it was obtained. For example, the file can go in `data/raw/`, with a source log identifying its address, release, retrieval date, and any selections or requests used. It should also retain earlier releases that support reported results.

If the collection will recur, have the agent turn what it learned into a saved script with explicit inputs and output locations. It may use a direct download, an API, or automated browser actions. The script should respect the service's limits on the number and frequency of requests and report failures, including an unexpected change in the data format or coverage. The research guide's [acquisition guidance](https://dss-agentic-research.pages.dev/chapters/data-acquisition.html#acquisition-ladder) explains how to choose a repeatable method.

::: {#prompt-collect-web-data .prompt}
> Obtain the 2024 population counts for every region from the public statistics portal I identified. Use a permitted API or export if available; inspect the website if needed to find the correct release. Confirm the year, geographic coverage, and population measure. Preserve the original download in `data/raw/` and record the source address, release, date, and selections in a source log. Check representative values and missing or duplicate regions. Create a reusable collection script with the year as an input, explicit output locations, the service's request limits, and clear failure reporting. If collection requires multiple requests, check a small retrieval before collecting the full set. Record the command and setup in `README.md` and use that script for future updates.
:::

## Save the checks and collection instructions {#save-browser-work-instructions}

For website work, have the agent add a "Website checks" section to `README.md`, the project's plain-text overview. It should record how to start and open the preview, which pages and controls to check, and the expected behavior. A recurring check, such as changing the year and verifying the displayed results, can be saved as a browser test that the agent runs after relevant changes.

For data collection, have it add a "Data collection" section identifying the source, collection command, inputs, and output locations. It should explain any personal sign-in, request limits, and what to do if collection fails. Have it record the browser or collection software and its version, with the configuration needed to run it again. Ask the agent to maintain these instructions and the source log as the collection changes; the research guide's [data-provenance section](https://dss-agentic-research.pages.dev/chapters/data-acquisition.html#data-provenance) explains the retained records in more detail.

[^tk-browser-api]: API stands for *application programming interface*, a way for a program to request data or operations directly. An export supplies a downloadable file, such as CSV (comma-separated values), a plain-text table format. If access requires an API key, use [Chapter 12: Keep credentials out of research files: 1Password and direnv](#credentials) to keep it separate from collection code and saved request records.
